'''''Hesperocyparis lusitanica''''', the '''Mexican cypress''', '''cedar-of-Goa''' or '''Goa cedar''', is a species of [[conifer]] in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]], native to [[Mexico]] and [[Central America]] ([[Guatemala]], [[El Salvador]] and [[Honduras]]). It has also been introduced to [[Belize]], [[Costa Rica]] and [[Nicaragua]], growing at {{convert|1200|-|3000|m|ft}} altitude.

The scientific name ''lusitanica'' (of [[Portugal]]) refers to its very early cultivation there, with plants imported from Mexico to the monastery at [[Buçaco Forest|Buçaco]], near [[Coimbra]] in Portugal in about 1634; these trees were already over 130 years old when the species was botanically described by [[Philip Miller|Miller]] in 1768.

In Mexico, the tree is also known as ''cedro blanco'' (white cedar) or ''teotlate''.

==Description==
''Hesperocyparis lusitanica'' is a [[conifer|coniferous]] tree with a conic to ovoid-conic crown, growing to 40 m tall. The foliage grows in dense sprays, dark green to somewhat yellow-green in colour. The leaves are scale-like, 2–5 mm long, and produced on rounded (not flattened) shoots. The seed [[conifer cone|cones]] are globose to oblong, 10–20 mm long, with four to 10 scales, green at first, maturing brown or grey-brown about 25 months after pollination.

The cones may either open at maturity to release the seeds, or remain closed for several years, only opening after the parent tree is killed in a [[wildfire]], allowing the [[seed]]s to colonise the bare ground exposed by the fire. The male cones are 3–4 mm long, and release pollen in late winter to early spring (February–March in the northern hemisphere). In most of its natural environment the rainfall occurs with more quantity in summer.

==Taxonomy==
''Hesperocyparis lusitanica'' was given its first scientific name by the botanist [[Philip Miller]] who named it ''Cupressus lusitanica'' in 1768,<ref name="POWO" /> because he described it from collections made in Portugal.<ref name="Gymnosperm DB">{{cite web |last1=Earle |first1=Christopher J. |title=''Hesperocyparis lusitanica'' (Mexican cypress) description |url=https://www.conifers.org/cu/Hesperocyparis_lusitanica.php |website=The Gymnosperm Database |access-date=25 February 2024 |date=17 December 2023}}</ref> The species has a large number of [[synonym (botany)|synonyms]] and the species ''[[Hesperocyparis benthamii]]'' has been treated as [[variety (botany)|variety]] or [[subspecies]] of ''H. lusitanica''.<ref>{{cite POWO |id=60451549-2 |title=''Hesperocyparis benthamii'' (Endl.) Bartel |access-date=25 February 2024}}</ref> In 2009 a paper was published moving this species and most of the New World ''[[Cupressus]]'' to the new genus ''[[Hesperocyparis]]''.<ref name="POWO" /> {{As of|2024}} this is listed as the accepted species name with no subspecies or varieties by [[Plants of the World Online]],<ref name="POWO" /> [[World Flora Online]],<ref>{{Cite WFO |title=''Hesperocyparis lusitanica'' (Mill.) Bartel |id=0000912972 |access-date=25 February 2024}}</ref> and the Gymnosperm Database.<ref name="Gymnosperm DB" />

==Cultivation and uses==
Fast-growing and drought tolerant, but only slightly frost tolerant, ''Hesperocyparis lusitanica'' has been introduced from Mexico to different parts of the world like New Zealand.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Kimberley |first1=Mark Owen |last2=Watt |first2=Michael Stuart |date=January 2023 |title=Growth Models for Even-Aged Stands of Hesperocyparis macrocarpa and Hesperocyparis lusitanica |journal=Forests |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |page=105 |doi=10.3390/f14010105 |doi-access=free |issn=1999-4907}}</ref> It is widely cultivated, both as an [[ornamental tree]] and for [[timber]] production, in warm, temperate and subtropical regions around the world. Trees have not been selected for cultivation from northern Mexico populations, which have a heavy drought endurance.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Felger |first1=Richard S. |last2=Johnson |first2=Matthew B. |last3=Wilson |first3=Michael F. |date=2001 |title=The trees of Sonora, Mexico |place=New York<!--sic --> |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0-19-512891-5}}</ref>

===Locations===
Its cultivation and subsequent [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalisation]] in parts of southern [[Asia]] has caused a degree of confusion with native ''Cupressus'' species in that region; plants sold by nurseries under the names of Asian species such as ''[[Cupressus torulosa]]'' often prove to be this species.

It has been planted widely for commercial production: at high altitudes in [[Colombia]] ({{cvt|3300|m|ft|disp=comma}}), [[Bolivia]], [[Ethiopia]] and [[South Africa]], and near sea level throughout [[New Zealand]].<ref name=":0" /> In [[Colombia]] trees are planted to form [[windbreak]] hedges and for preventing soil erosion on slopes. It has been planted by [[Tanzania]]n mountain farmers for soil preservation and commercial use since the 1990s.<ref>UEDA Gen, ''The Regional System of the Mountain People: Place, Household, and the Communal in Rural Tanzania'' (Japanese language), Tohoku University Press, 2011, Sendai, Japan, pp.348 - 351. (上田元『山の民の地域システム　タンザニア農村の場所・世帯・共同性』、東北大学出版会、2011年)</ref>

It has been planted as an ornamental tree near sea level in temperate climates and has done very well in [[Portugal]], [[Buenos Aires Province]] in [[Argentina]]; [[Austin, Texas]] and the [[British Isles]] where it can reach a height of 30 m (90 feet).

It is being planted in the Argentine province of [[San Luis Province|San Luis]],<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.rama.com.ar/rama_newasp/PaginasIngles/Especies.asp?itemMenu=6&subitemMenu=12
| title=Mexican conifers in San Luis Province, Argentina}}</ref> [[Argentina]] at {{cvt|1500|m|ft}} above sea level to create artificial forests in a land originally lacking them in a very similar climate to that of its native habitat.
